extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, lexicographers, and careful writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, fixing, and evaluating definitions and the connotation/denotation of terms in scientific and common language. Emphasizes principles to preserve usage, select characteristic marks, and avoid pernicious extensions or losses of meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve received denotation when fixing connotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When fixing the connotation of a concrete name, the definition should not deviate from but should agree (as far as it goes) with the vague and fluctuating connotation which the term already had; give an exact connotation without rendering received assertions inadmissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer definitions that remain in agreement with the word's current use. If you can fix the connotation without making previously true propositions false, do so—this is vulgarly called 'defining not the name but the thing.' If not possible, be explicit about the change and its consequences. Anti-pattern: imposing a precise technical meaning that contradicts established usage and thereby invalidates accepted propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain common attributes by comparison and induction
rubrics_metrics.description: To fix a connotation you must first ascertain in what particulars the objects classed together agree; this requires comparison 'feature by feature and property by property' and frequently strictly inductive work to discover unobvious agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base definitions on objective examination of the things denoted: list common properties, use observation/experimentation where necessary. Examples: examining motions to define 'uniform force.' Scoring note: stronger definitions rest on demonstrable common attributes rather than mere intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select marks that are known and diagnostically powerful
rubrics_metrics.description: From the many common properties select those which are well known and familiarly predicated, but crucially those on which many other properties depend or which are sure marks of them, so that many others follow by inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer properties that serve as reliable indicators (marks) of the rest of the class's properties; choose features that enable inference and classification. Anti-pattern: choosing superficially familiar properties that don't distinguish the class or fail to imply others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give preference to properties that serve scientific propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A definition has scientific value only when it is associated with some proposition or principle it is meant to express; definitions should be proposed to serve an immediate use in enunciating truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before fixing a definition ask 'what principle does this serve to enunciate?' Examples: defining 'uniform force' in a way that preserves the proposition that gravity is uniform; defining 'momentum' to express conservation in collisions. Anti-pattern: abstractly defining a term with no connection to any substantive proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions are part of discovery and require sagacity
rubrics_metrics.description: To define so that a definition has scientific value requires a portion of the sagacity by which truth is detected; the definition presupposes that a decided step in knowledge has been made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat definition as an intellectual achievement tied to understanding; avoid treating it as a mechanical or purely linguistic task. Example: establishing that momentum equals mass times velocity followed experimental insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to define by non-obvious but best-marking properties
rubrics_metrics.description: It is often necessary to define the class by some property not familiarly known, provided that property be the best mark of the other common properties (e.g., De Blainville defining life by incessant decomposition and recomposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reject less obvious attributes if they more accurately and usefully identify the class; weigh diagnostic power over familiarity. Anti-pattern: insisting only on obvious features at the expense of theoretical fruitfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow definitions to evolve with scientific progress
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to frame a perfect set of definitions until the theory of the subject is perfect; as science advances, definitions should be progressive and adjusted to new knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revisit and revise definitions when empirical or theoretical advances reveal better marks or causal relations. Scoring note: durable definitions are those adaptable to improved understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer restricting denotation rather than extending it when remedying vagueness
rubrics_metrics.description: When a word is vague, in fixing its connotation it is often better to restrict the denotation—excluding some common applications—than to extend it to cover all agreeable cases (example: 'beautiful' should be restricted so as not to reduce it to mere 'agreeableness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If forced to narrow or broaden a term, favor preserving distinctive nuances by narrowing; anti-pattern: broadening a vague term so that it loses the qualities it was meant to highlight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not discard historical connotations without strong grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting to rectify a vague term by giving it a fixed connotation, take care not to discard (unless advisedly and on the ground of deeper knowledge) any portion of the connotation the word previously carried, since language conserves ancient experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the history and traditional uses of a term before redefining it; preserving past connotations keeps alive useful insights. Anti-pattern: redefining terms based only on present minimal usage and thereby obliterating historical meanings and associated truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the history of a word before fixing its meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever seeks to introduce a more correct use of a term should possess an accurate acquaintance with the history of the particular word and of the opinions it served to express; to be qualified to define the name we must know what has ever been known of the properties of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace prior senses, the propositions formerly expressed, and consequences of changing the meaning. Example: if a new definition would render any formerly generally-held proposition false, one must be sure the older understanding was erroneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware transitive extensions and blended meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Words often acquire 'transitive' applications by gradual extension from one object to another via intermediate affinities; such transference can produce blended meanings where no single common property remains (e.g., 'beautiful').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect when multiple derived senses have coalesced; if meanings have become inextricably blended, recognize that a single precise definition may be impossible. Anti-pattern: assuming all varieties of a term must reduce to a single genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication as an antidote to semantic corrosion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because words in habitual use tend to call up only one or two aspects of their original complex meaning, the habit of predicating of the name all the various properties originally connoted helps keep up the association and prevents loss of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit predication (state properties explicitly in propositions) to preserve the fuller meaning of terms across generations. Practical tip: teach and repeat substantive predicates associated with key terms to keep their meanings alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fixing definitions at moments of minimal meaning (freeze of decline)
rubrics_metrics.description: When words have lost part of their significance, persons aiming for definite language may fix the name according to its weakest contemporary connotation, thereby extending denotation beyond former bounds and treating ancient propositions as prejudices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt a rigid definition based on the 'smallest quantity of meaning' current at a low point of understanding; doing so can accelerate loss of valuable meanings and impede recovery of older truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should be debated with respect to properties and causal relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing a good definition of a name already in use is a matter of discussion respecting not merely usage but the properties of things and even the origin (causal relations) of those properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage substantive discussion on which properties are intrinsic, which are causally prior, and how they relate before settling on a definition. Scoring note: definitions grounded in causal/deductive relations are preferable.
